newsitem.title: CHINA: China says state losses up but economy strong.
newsitem.headline: China says state losses up but economy strong.

text.p: China said losses in its ailing state industry jumped sharply last year but the red ink was far from crippling the nation's robust economy.
It also defended its statistics, saying that some economic data might be inaccurate, but for the most part its figures were reliable.
"There were state companies that lost money but this has not fundamentally shaken the economy," said Zhang Sai, director of the State Statistical Bureau.
Zhang told reporters that only about one-third of state companies lost money last year, though their losses were up from the year before.
"There is a perception that no state companies are any good," said Zhang. "This is not true."
The bureau's chief economist Qiu Xiaohua said losses of state firms operating in the red reached 72.7 billion yuan ($8.75 billion) last year, an increase of 37.5 percent over 1995.
He said losses of all companies not making a profit, including those outside the state sector, stood at 123.4 billion yuan, up 34.9 percent.

Officials said that the economy, which grew 9.7 percent last year, was healthy enough to compensate for the losses, which reflected only a small -- though highly visible -- part of the overall economic picture.
Bureau officials said that as state companies tended to be large, any layoffs or failure to pay wages had the potential for substantial political impact.
Many of China's big state companies are grossly overstaffed and cannot turn a profit unless they trim their payrolls.
Bureau officials said that one in five state companies operating in the red was a persistent money loser due to poor management or lagging technology.
"These may have to be driven out of the market," said economist Qiu.
But large-scale layoffs are politically unacceptable because they are seen as a threat to stability.

The officials said some 10 million workers had been removed from the payrolls of state firms due to retrenchments last year and more than half had found new jobs elsewhere. There were no further details on the figures.
But officials were defensive about the integrity of their published data.
"The quality of statistics is a big issue. There are problems with micro-economic figures," said Zhang. "Some figures are exaggerated or falsified."
But he countered that the statistical bureau was confident that it was able to catch problem figures or adjust for such distortions.
"Our macro-economic statistics are reliable," he said. ($1 = 8.3 yuan)
